1:
The chapter opens on an oath the narrative never reported. Ellicott marks the gap: the circumstance was not mentioned in the account of the proceedings at Mizpeh, and it is clear from the sequel that this was not merely an oath but a vow under a curse, like that of the men who bound themselves to kill Paul. Clarke says the same, and reads it as evidence that the war began with a settled determination to destroy the Benjamites utterly: if any escaped the sword no man might give him a daughter, and by that means the remnant must soon have been annihilated. Gill sets it in order: the tribes convened at Mizpeh, heard the Levite's account, demanded the men of Gibeah, found the demand refused and war preparing, resolved on destroying Gibeah and every city that had sent out men against them, and then bound themselves to treat the survivors as heathens and not intermarry with them. Henry supplies a second oath of the same period, sworn while the convention was still filling up: the great execration they called the Cherem, devoting to destruction any city that failed to send its representatives and quota. Refusal, they judged, showed no indignation at the crime, no concern to secure the nation from God's judgments by doing justice, and no regard for a common summons.

Henry is careful about what the marriage oath was for. It bound only the thousands then present and those they represented, not their posterity, and was made an article of the war with no design to extirpate the tribe. The intent was that the actual actors and abettors of the villainy be treated like the devoted nations of Canaan, whom Israel was not only obliged to destroy but forbidden to marry. Such men had also shown themselves unworthy to match with a daughter of Israel, having been so barbarous to one of the tender sex — than which nothing could be more base, nor any surer sign given of a mind wholly lost to honour. He adds a shrewd note on how the fury was raised: the Levite's sending the mangled pieces of his wife's body round the tribes inflamed them more than any account of the fact could have done, however well attested — so much does the eye affect the heart.

Keil weighs the outcome against the cause and finds the war outran its warrant. The severity of the tribes had cut Benjamin to six hundred men and brought it within reach of extermination, and that went to the heart of the congregation. He grants the beginning was sound — the resolution to punish the wickedness of Gibeah with the full severity of the law was urged by nothing but the duty to root the evil out, the war was justified by the tribe's taking the culprits' side, and it had the Lord's approval. But after two defeats at Benjamin's hands, personal revenge disturbed the righteous cause and carried the warriors into a war of extermination neither commanded by the law nor justified by the circumstances. Henry reaches the same judgment through their grief. The tide of anger before ran no higher than the tide of sorrow after; they repented for Benjamin their brother — not of their zeal against the sin, since there is a holy indignation which is a fruit of godly sorrow, but of carrying the matter further than was just, cutting off husbandmen and shepherds, women and children, when it had been enough to destroy those found in arms. From this he draws four maxims: that there may be over-doing in well-doing, and no divinity is good that swallows up humanity; that even necessary justice should be done with compassion, since God does not punish with delight; that strong passions make work for repentance; and that a civil war admits no triumph, because whichever side wins the community loses.
2:
Where the people went to weep is disputed. Gill denies the house of God means Bethel, as the Targum and Septuagint took it, and places the scene at Shiloh, where tabernacle and ark then stood; they came, he says, not to give thanks for the victory but to lament Benjamin's case and take counsel how to repair the loss. Clarke reads the Hebrew flatly as Bethel, with the Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic behind him, and Ellicott agrees, citing the two earlier visits. Keil agrees: the men assembled for the war returned to Bethel to weep a day before God over what the war had cost the congregation. On the temper of that weeping they converge. Clarke puts it shortly — revenge satisfied, reflection brings contrition; Ellicott notes they had wept before, after their defeat, but were now remorseful for those they had then been pledged to destroy. Clarke will not let the lament pass as a real question. Why is this come to pass, he calls impertinent, since they knew perfectly well how: it was right that Gibeah be punished and right that those who vindicated them share it, but they carried revenge too far and set out to exterminate man and beast alike. Ellicott answers that it is no inquiry into a cause too patent to need one, but a wail of regret carrying a prayer to be shown how the calamity might be met; and in the threefold repetition of the name Israel he finds a nation that had not lost its sense of corporate unity, however often dissension tore it. Their wild justice, he adds, is mingled with a still wilder mercy.

The altar built next morning is a difficulty every voice feels. Keil grants there is something strange in erecting one at Bethel, and reads it as a practical expression of their wish, since they knew nothing could succeed without reconciliation to the Lord and a return to the fellowship of his grace. Gill has them rising early after fasting and prayer, hoping that in the way of duty the difficulty would be removed. Clarke draws the sharper inference: needing to build one shows the place was no regular sanctuary, and the act was not according to law — but there was neither king nor law among them, and each did what seemed right in his own eyes. Ellicott collects parallels — David at Araunah's threshing-floor, Solomon at Gibeon — and suggests the multitude of sacrifices needed for the holocausts and the people's food may have made a second altar necessary; then admits some other reason probably lies behind it which we do not know.

Then the oath becomes an expedient. Ellicott identifies its spirit with the curse on Meroz, who came not to the help of the Lord, and reads the search for defaulters shrewdly: the victories had been so complete that the people were sick with slaughter, and inquired after absentees only to soften their own rash vow — which, taken with the curse, had plainly meant to annihilate the tribe. Gill states the mechanism: Jabesh-gilead, having stayed away from Mizpeh, had never sworn to withhold their daughters, so wives might be taken thence without breaking any oath. Clarke infers that Benjamin's women and children had all been massacred deliberately, so that any survivor should find neither wife nor daughter; and he will not soften the sequel, in which twelve thousand men killed every male and every married woman of Jabesh — the crime of Gibeah was of the deepest dye, the punishment ran to a criminal excess taking guilty and innocent together, and the remedy was equally abominable. Ellicott closes more gently, tracing Jabesh afterwards: its peril first roused Saul, and the men of Jabesh alone saved the bodies of Saul and Jonathan from the wall of Bethshan and earned David's blessing — proof the town recovered from the extermination inflicted here.
9:
The muster that convicts Jabesh-gilead Gill treats lightly: the people were numbered to learn who had come up and who had not, and particularly whether the men of Jabesh had, an information having been laid against them. Ellicott doubts a second numbering is meant at all. In the tally made at Mizpeh the absence of one town's inhabitants might well have escaped notice, and it would now be enough to consult the lists already drawn. On the force sent out the texts differ: Gill notes the Vulgate has ten thousand where the Hebrew, Targum, Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic read twelve, Josephus with them, and passes on Bunting's estimate that the place lay fifty-two miles from Shiloh. Ellicott takes the twelve thousand to mean a thousand valiant men from each tribe, as in the war against Midian in which Balaam was killed and at which Phinehas was present. Keil states the commission and its limit together: they were to smite the inhabitants with the sword, women and children included, but under the more precise instruction to ban every male and every woman who had known man — which implied that virgins who had not should be spared.

Four hundred such were found, and Gill will not pretend the arithmetic of conscience is clear. How it was that the men of Israel did not think themselves bound by their oath to put these to death along with the rest, he says, is not easy to say: whether they judged the necessity of the case excused it, or had a dispensation from the Lord on consulting him. He is equally candid about how they were identified — by age, by their unmarried state and by common report, unless one supposes they were examined by matrons. Ellicott worries at the grammar and reaches a humane conclusion. The pronoun in they brought them is masculine though the virgins must be meant; he compares the Greek idiom by which a woman speaking of herself in the plural uses the masculine, admits no other trace of it in Hebrew, then gives his real reason — we can hardly suppose captives were brought all the way to Shiloh and there killed in cold blood under the ban. He adds that the standing camp appears to have moved to Shiloh once the war was over, that being the more central seat of the tabernacle, and puzzles over the added clause in the land of Canaan, which Jabesh lying in Gilead does not seem enough to account for.

Then the overture to the rock Rimmon. Clarke and Ellicott agree on the phrase: to call peaceably is to proclaim peace, and Clarke spells out what the proclamation conveyed — that the enmity was all over and the fugitives might safely leave their stronghold. Gill has the six hundred returning with the messengers at once, putting confidence in the assurances given them. But the remedy falls short, and all three arithmetics agree. Clarke counts it out plainly: six hundred men at Rimmon and only four hundred women saved from Jabesh, so two hundred still wanting; Ellicott says the same; Keil explains why no wives could be found nearer home, since out of Benjamin every woman was destroyed in the ruthless slaughter of the whole tribe, and notes that the writer now repeats the earlier verses about the people's grief with only a slight change of expression, by way of introducing what follows. On the last words Ellicott is sharpest. The breach was caused by their own headstrong fury and unreasoning passion, righteous though the original cause had been; yet in the Hebrew conception the results even of man's sin and folly are referred to Jehovah as overruling them. It was therefore needless, and not quite honest, of Jerome to drop the Lord from the Vulgate.
16:
Four hundred wives found and two hundred men still wanting, the elders reopen the question. Keil states their principle: Benjamin must survive as a tribe, so the tribe-land remains an independent possession for those who escaped, and they must be helped to wives — which the other tribes could not do directly, the oath standing in the way, so that hardly any course was left but to let them seize wives themselves. Gill works out the property logic. The inheritance had been divided by lot to Benjamin and belonged to that tribe only; it now devolved of right on these six hundred, and their number must be increased that they might occupy what was theirs and rebuild it. Ellicott renders the clause as a grant rather than a necessity — possession of the remnant shall be for Benjamin, or as Josephus has it, we give you leave to take the whole land. He then finds the repair incomplete: Benjamin never quite recovered, and though it gave Israel the second judge and the first king and was often honoured by Samuel's residence, it became a satellite of the more powerful Judah — in which quiescence Ellicott sees part of the blessing Moses pronounced on the tribe.

On the vow itself Ellicott is severe, and the severity is the heart of the chapter: they keep it in the letter while breaking it in the spirit. The sense of the ban's binding force was intensely strong, but as so often among rude peoples they imagined it enough to keep it literally while violating it in effect — as Themison in Herodotus, sworn to throw Phronima into the sea when the intent was that she drown, threw her in and had her drawn out again. Their want of moral enlightenment showed there, and more in ever taking so horrible an oath, which involved the butchery of innocent men and of still more innocent women and children. His judgment compresses to a sentence: the guilt of breaking a guilty vow is only the original guilt of ever having made it. What they should have done was not to bathe their hands in more fraternal blood but to pray God forgive the brutal vehemence that disgraced a righteous cause, and let the remnant intermarry with them again. Henry, less fierce, reaches the same place — a sorry salvo is better than none to save an oath, but far better to be cautious in vowing, so that there be no need afterwards to say before the angel that it was an error. The less consideration goes into a vow, he adds, the more is needed afterwards to keep it.

The opportunity was a yearly feast at Shiloh; which, nobody will say. Clarke names none of the three, observing only that all fell when the vines were in full leaf, so the Benjaminites could hide there; Ellicott thinks a local feast unlikely and tabernacles most natural, and Henry follows Bishop Patrick in making it tabernacles, the only season at which Jewish virgins might dance — and then not for recreation but to express holy joy, as David danced before the ark. The dancing, Henry insists, was modest: not mixed, no men joining, no married women forgetting their gravity. Yet it left them easy prey, whence Bishop Hall observed that the ambushes of evil spirits carry many souls from dancing to a fearful desolation. The elaborate description of Shiloh's site divides the commentators. Clarke sees no reason for such minuteness unless the feast was that year held somewhere unusual, and the Benjaminites, shut up in Rimmon, needed exact directions. Ellicott judges it a later scribe's marginal gloss, since it interrupts the elders' speech and would have been needless to men standing at Shiloh itself — but by then Shiloh had long been desolate, and this addition alone has let us identify the site in the modern Seilun.
21:
Gill explains why the daughters of Shiloh were there to take. Only males were obliged to appear at the feast, but women might come if they wished, and many did; those of Shiloh, living where the tabernacle stood, always attended with joy, dancing as an expression of religious gladness, like Miriam. They danced by themselves, not with men, which made them the easier to seize. Ellicott takes these for the dances of the vintage festival, and points to a fountain in a narrow dale near Shiloh as probably the scene; he dismisses as needless the conjecture that the dances commemorated Egypt's defeat. He also widens who those daughters were. There seems to have been no regular town at Shiloh — no extensive ruins are traceable — but a community bound to the tabernacle's service, so the phrase would take in many women employed about it, not only worshippers; traces of such attendants, he grants, are commoner in Jewish tradition than in Scripture. Clarke states the order plainly: let each of the two hundred seize and carry off a woman, whom he is from that hour to consider his wife.

The verse promising to pacify the fathers is the obscurest here, and Clarke says so before laying the versions side by side. The Vulgate makes the elders plead that the Benjaminites did not take these women as victors take captives, but asked and were refused, so the fault lies with the fathers — a reading in which Clarke suspects Jerome had the Sabines in mind. Houbigant has the elders argue that the Benjaminites took no wives with them to the war, and unless the women are now conceded the refusers will be the sinners. The Authorised reading rests the plea on Israel's own failure to spare Benjamin's women, so the concession asked obliges Israel more than Benjamin. Clarke leaves the reader to choose, allowing the Vulgate a good sense but thinking Houbigant comes nearest. Keil reconstructs it as words the elders will speak in the Benjaminites' name to the complaining relatives; Ellicott renders the opening not be favourable to them but present them to us. He thinks the parents may have been the sooner consoled because the land now held by six hundred far exceeded their wants, they having become possessors of a whole tribe's lot — and notes we are left to assume the appeal succeeded.

The Benjaminites took their two hundred, returned home, rebuilt the burnt towns and dwelt in them. Clarke thinks they behaved honourably afterwards, and notes the women came to an inheritance at least equal to their own, since none of Benjamin's land was alienated and six hundred men now shared what had belonged to many thousands. Keil closes on the two remarks — the congregation dispersed, every man to his tribe; and in those days there was no king in Israel — and notes the writer never says whether the fathers complained, because it would have made no difference to the facts. Gill dates the whole by that line: Joshua was dead and no judge had yet risen, so all that fills these last chapters falls between. Clarke will not let the book end without a disclaimer. Let no one suppose the writer justifies these atrocities by relating them; they cannot be justified, and his impartiality in recording what was so much to his country's discredit is itself the strongest proof of authenticity. He then sets the Roman parallel beside it, Romulus seizing the Sabine women at the feast of Neptune after his neighbours refused him intermarriage — an act which brought on wars the stolen women at last mediated. Ellicott ends more hopefully: the closing formula is added once more as an apology for the lawless crimes, evaded vows and unhallowed excesses the historian has faithfully narrated; out of these depths the judges partially raised their countrymen until the nation was ripe for monarchy.
